The onset of first feeding follows shortly after yolk-sac resorption, marking the transition to an exotrophic larval existence. This species exhibits a protandrous hermaphroditic social system, wherein all individuals initially mature as males and later may transition to female. The standard length at which individuals attain puberty, marking the onset of functional male reproductive capacity, is approximately 6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6 centimeters], a size commonly reached within the first year of benthic life.

Field surveys indicate that these size thresholds are relatively stable across the species' wide geographical range, from the Persian Gulf to the western Pacific.

This high fecundity per event is characteristic of many small-bodied marine teleosts that produce pelagic larvae, offsetting the substantial mortality experienced during the planktonic phase. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, typically laid in a dense monolayer on a cleaned substrate near the host anemone, where they are aggressively guarded and aerated by the resident male. Parental care is exclusively male, with the female defending the territory perimeter. Hatching synchrony is high, with most embryos emerging within a single evening, coinciding with dusk to reduce predation pressure on the emerging prolarvae.

The life span is considerably longer than that of many other tropical reef fishes of comparable body size, likely reflecting the reduced predation risk afforded by the stinging tentacles of its anemone host and the stable food resources available within its territory. Field-marking studies have confirmed that individuals can persist within the same social group for over a decade, with the breeding female being the oldest member. This longevity strategy, combined with the ability to undergo sex change, ensures reproductive continuity within the social unit when the dominant female is lost.
